concepts.name: Territorial extent and distribution of legislative subjects
concepts.description: Territorial limits of Central and state laws, the three lists of the Seventh Schedule, their numbers, residuary powers, predominance and GST.
concepts.idea: The Constitution divides legislative subjects three ways, secures Union predominance and vests residuary power in Parliament.
concepts.rule: Parliament can legislate for the whole or any part of India and alone makes extra-territorial laws, while a state law applies outside the state only with a sufficient nexus (p.222). The President makes regulations for certain union territories, and the Governor or President can direct that an Act not apply to scheduled or tribal areas (p.222). The Union List has 98 subjects, the State List 59 and the Concurrent List 52, and the 42nd Amendment moved five subjects to the Concurrent List (pp.222-223). Residuary powers lie with Parliament, as in Canada, unlike the 1935 Act which gave them to the Governor-General (p.223). Union List prevails over State and Concurrent Lists and the Concurrent over the State List; a state law with Presidential assent prevails in that state but Parliament may override it later (p.223). The 101st Amendment gave concurrent GST powers and Parliament exclusive power over inter-state supplies (p.223).
concepts.example: A state law on a Concurrent subject that received Presidential assent prevails in that state until Parliament subsequently legislates on the same matter (p.223).

questions.q: The Constitution of India divides powers between the Centre and the states in several spheres. Which one of the following powers is NOT divided between them?
questions.e: The Constitution divides all powers (legislative, executive and financial) between the Centre and the states, but there is no division of judicial power because an integrated judicial system enforces both Central and state laws.
w: Legislative power is divided by the three lists of the Seventh Schedule.
Executive power is divided between the Centre and the states, broadly on the lines of legislative power.
Financial power is divided, as the taxing powers show.

concepts.name: Parliamentary legislation in the state field and the Centre's control over state legislation
concepts.description: The five situations in which Parliament legislates in the state field and the Centre's controls over state legislation.
concepts.idea: In abnormal situations the federal distribution bends towards Parliament, and the Centre also checks state bills.
concepts.rule: Parliament may legislate on State List matters (and GST) on a Rajya Sabha resolution backed by two-thirds of members present and voting, in force one year at a time and renewable (p.224). It may also do so during a national emergency, at the request of two or more states, to implement international agreements, and during President's rule (p.224). Laws under the Rajya Sabha resolution or emergency cease six months after they end, whereas a law made in President's rule continues and can be altered by the state legislature (pp.224-225). A state request makes the law applicable to the requesting states and operates as abdication of state power (p.224). The Centre controls state legislation through reservation of bills for the President, Article 304 sanction, financial emergency directions and Governor's ordinance limits (p.225).
concepts.example: The Geneva Convention Act, 1960 implements an international obligation, whereas the Prize Competition Act, 1955 was passed on state requests (p.224).

concepts.name: Administrative relations: executive power, directions and delegation
concepts.description: Distribution of executive power, obligations of states, Centre's directions, delegation, cooperation devices and emergency relations.
concepts.idea: Executive power follows legislative power, but states must not impede the Centre, backed by Article 365.
concepts.rule: The Centre's executive power covers Union List subjects and treaty rights, a state's covers the State List, and on Concurrent subjects it rests with the states unless Constitution or Parliament confers it on the Centre (pp.225-226). States must comply with Parliament's laws and not impede Central executive power; non-compliance with directions can lead to President's rule via Article 365 (p.226). The Centre may direct states on communications of national importance, railway protection, mother-tongue instruction and Scheduled Tribe schemes (p.226). Delegation is by agreement with consent, or by a law of Parliament without consent, which a state legislature cannot do (pp.226-227). Cooperation devices include water-dispute adjudication, the Inter-State Council (set up 1990) and full faith and credit (p.227). Emergencies and Article 355 increase Central control (p.229).
concepts.example: The Essential Commodities Act is made on a Concurrent subject yet vests executive power in the Centre (footnote 5, p.249).

concepts.idea: Several bodies tie the Centre and states together without dividing the administration entirely.
concepts.rule: The IAS, IPS and IFoS are recruited and trained by the Centre, controlled jointly, and form a single service with uniform pay; new services need a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 312 (p.227). They restrict state autonomy but are defended for standards, uniformity and liaison (p.228). A state PSC's members are appointed by the Governor and removed only by the President; Parliament can set up a Joint State PSC and the UPSC can serve states on request (p.228). India has an integrated judiciary, and Parliament can establish a common high court (p.228). Non-constitutional advisory bodies such as NITI Aayog and conferences like the governors' and chief ministers' conferences promote coordination (p.229).

concepts.name: Financial relations: taxing powers, tax revenues and GST
concepts.description: Taxing powers, their limits, the distribution of tax revenues after the 80th and 101st Amendments, non-tax revenue and the GST Council.
concepts.idea: Levy, collection and appropriation of taxes are separated across Articles 268 to 271 and GST.
concepts.rule: Parliament taxes Union List subjects, states taxes State List subjects, there are no tax entries in the Concurrent List except GST, and residuary taxes lie with Parliament (p.230). States face limits such as the Rs 2,500 profession tax ceiling (p.230). Article 268 duties are levied by the Centre and collected and appropriated by states; Article 269 taxes are assigned to states; Article 269A covers inter-state GST; Article 270 taxes are shared on Finance Commission advice; Article 271 surcharges go to the Centre alone (pp.231-232). The 80th Amendment followed the 10th Finance Commission's 29 per cent scheme and the 101st Amendment introduced GST (p.231). The GST Council under Article 279-A recommends rates, exemptions and model laws (pp.233-234).
concepts.example: Stamp duties on cheques and promissory notes are levied by the Centre but collected and appropriated by the state in which levied (p.231).

concepts.idea: Grants, the Finance Commission and immunities balance fiscal federalism.
concepts.rule: Article 275 statutory grants go to needy states on the Finance Commission's advice, while Article 282 grants are discretionary (p.233). The Finance Commission under Article 280 is quasi-judicial, constituted every fifth year or earlier, and is the balancing wheel of fiscal federalism (p.234). Certain tax bills need the President's recommendation and the CAG certifies net proceeds (pp.234-235). The Centre can borrow within or outside India, states only within India, and states need Central consent while Central loans are outstanding (p.235). Central property is exempt from state tax, state property from Central tax, but companies and local authorities are not exempt, and customs and excise duties are not covered by state immunity (pp.235-236). In a national emergency the President can reduce or cancel transfers, and in a financial emergency the Centre can direct salary reductions (p.236).

concepts.idea: After 1967 states demanded autonomy, producing a series of reports the Centre largely ignored.
concepts.rule: Relations were smooth till 1967; after Congress lost nine states, non-Congress governments demanded autonomy and resources (p.236). Fourteen tension areas are listed, from governors to Central agencies (pp.236-237). The First ARC (1966, Morarji Desai, then K. Hanumanthayya) reported in 1969 with 22 recommendations after a Setalvad study team, and no action followed (p.237). The Tamil Nadu Government's Rajamannar Committee (appointed 1969, reported 1971) recommended a permanent Finance Commission, omitting Articles 356, 357 and 365, and state residuary powers (pp.237-238). concepts.name: Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions
concepts.description: The Sarkaria Commission (1983-88) and the Punchhi Commission (2007-10): approach and key recommendations.
concepts.idea: Sarkaria worked within a strong Centre through functional changes, while Punchhi urged cooperative federalism with Union restraint and a few constitutional amendments.
concepts.rule: The three-member Sarkaria Commission (1983, reported 1988) found the constitutional arrangements sound, rejected curtailing the Centre, and made 247 recommendations, of which 180 were implemented, most importantly the Inter-State Council in 1990 (pp.238-240). It recommended sparing use of Article 356, strengthened All-India Services and reactivated zonal councils (p.239). The Punchhi Commission (2007, reported 2010, 1,456 pages) concluded cooperative federalism was the key and made over 310 recommendations (p.240). They covered governors' tenure and selection, hung-assembly guidelines, localised emergency, new All-India Services and fiscal reforms (pp.241-244).
concepts.example: Sarkaria wanted the NDC renamed the National Economic and Development Council, while Punchhi proposed a framework for localised emergency (pp.239, 242).
